## [1]{.num} Install three free programs {#before}

extract-text needs three programs that it does not install itself.

- **poppler** opens PDF files.
- **tesseract** reads scanned pages (OCR).
- **Python 3.10 or newer** runs the engine, the part of extract-text that reads the documents. The Python that comes with a Mac is older.

You install them once, in a terminal window. Find your computer below. You need the internet only to install. After that, extract-text runs with the network unplugged.

::: {.note}
**Check your system first, and update it if it is old.**

- **Mac.** Open the Apple menu and choose About This Mac. You need macOS 15 (Sequoia) or later, and a line that reads "Chip: Apple M1" or later. Homebrew, the installer used below, keeps ready-made copies of poppler, tesseract, and Python only for the three newest versions of macOS on Apple chips (in November 2026: macOS 15, 26, and 27). On macOS 14 or older, or on an Intel Mac, it prints a warning and tries to build each program from its source code, which is slow and can fail, as it did for one of our testers on macOS 14. Update macOS first, in System Settings, General, Software Update. For a Mac that cannot be updated, Homebrew's own advice is MacPorts, which we have not tested.
- **Windows.** Press the Windows key, type `winver`, and press Enter. Windows 11 works with everything on this page. On Windows 10, the three programs and R need version 1809 or later, and the current RStudio lists Windows 11 only.
:::

::: {.os-group}
### Mac

1. Open Terminal. Press Command and Space, type Terminal, and press Return.
2. Install [Homebrew](https://brew.sh){target="_blank" rel="noopener noreferrer"} if you do not have it. Homebrew is a free program that installs other programs. Its page gives one line to paste into Terminal.
3. Run this line.

```bash
brew install poppler tesseract python
```
:::

::: {.os-group}
### Windows

1. Open PowerShell. Press the Windows key, type PowerShell, and press Enter.
2. Run these three lines, one at a time.

```powershell
winget install oschwartz10612.Poppler
winget install UB-Mannheim.TesseractOCR
winget install Python.Python.3.12
```

3. Add tesseract to your PATH, which its installer does not do. Open Start, type "Edit environment variables for your account", and open it. Select Path, choose Edit, choose New, and enter `C:\Program Files\Tesseract-OCR`.
4. Restart RStudio if it is open. If you work at a terminal, close PowerShell and open it again, so that it sees the new PATH.
:::

::: {.os-group}
### Linux (Debian or Ubuntu)

Run this line in a terminal.

```bash
sudo apt install poppler-utils tesseract-ocr python3 python3-venv
```
:::

**If you already have some of these,** check before you install. Run `which pdftoppm tesseract python3` in Terminal on a Mac or Linux, or `where.exe pdftoppm tesseract python` in PowerShell on Windows. A program you have prints a path. On a Mac, `brew install` on a program you already have upgrades it and everything that depends on it, which can be a large download.

On a work computer of any kind, these installs may need your IT department. Ask for poppler, tesseract, and Python 3.10 or newer, and send them [For your IT department](https://github.com/evictionresearch/extract-text/blob/main/docs/it_checklist.md){target="_blank" rel="noopener noreferrer"}, which lists each program, where it comes from, and what the rest of the install does.

## [2]{.num} Install extract-text {#install}

::::: {.tabs}
:::: {.tab data-tab="r"}
In RStudio, run these lines. They install extract-text, check that R can find Python, and then install the engine, the part of extract-text that reads the documents. You do this once per computer.

```r
install.packages(c("remotes", "dplyr"))
remotes::install_github("evictionresearch/extract-text", subdir = "r")

library(extracttext)

# A check before the engine is installed. It should print the path of a
# Python, 3.10 or newer. NULL means R found none: go back to step 1,
# restart RStudio, and run this block again.
reticulate::virtualenv_starter(">=3.10")

extracttext_install()
```

The install, `extracttext_install()`, puts the engine in a folder of its own inside your user folder. It asks for no administrator password. It prints many lines as it works, and you can ignore them unless it ends with the word Error. On a fast connection it takes under a minute. It is finished when the Console shows "Done. Restart R, then run extracttext_doctor()." **Restart R** when it finishes, so the package finds the engine. In RStudio, choose Session, then Restart R. Then check your setup.

```r
library(extracttext)
library(dplyr)

extracttext_doctor()
```

The last line of the checkup should be this one.

```{.output}
Ready: the deterministic engine can run.
```

The checkup lists poppler and tesseract with the folder it found each in. It reports Ollama as missing, and that is fine. Ollama belongs to the experimental AI engine, which these steps do not use. If the checkup says the Python engine is not installed, see [If something goes wrong](#help).
::::

:::: {.tab data-tab="terminal"}
In the terminal, run these lines. They make a private Python environment for the engine, turn it on, and install extract-text into it. You do this once per computer. Python from Homebrew on a Mac, and from Debian or Ubuntu, refuses a plain `pip install` outside an environment like this one.

```bash
python3 -m venv ~/extract-text-env
source ~/extract-text-env/bin/activate
pip install "extract-text @ https://github.com/evictionresearch/extract-text/archive/main.zip#subdirectory=python"
```

On Windows, skip the first two lines. The Python that step 1 installs accepts the `pip install` line as it is. On a Mac or Linux, run the `source` line again in every new terminal window, before any `extract-text` command. Then check your setup.

```bash
extract-text doctor
```

The last line of the checkup should be this one.

```{.output}
Ready: the deterministic engine can run.
```

The checkup lists poppler and tesseract with the folder it found each in. It reports Ollama as missing, and that is fine. Ollama belongs to the experimental AI engine, which these steps do not use. If the terminal answers "command not found", see [If something goes wrong](#help).
::::

:::: {.tab data-tab="python"}
The engine is a Python package, so the install is the same as at a terminal. Run these lines in a terminal window. They make a private Python environment for the engine, turn it on, and install extract-text into it. You do this once per computer. Python from Homebrew on a Mac, and from Debian or Ubuntu, refuses a plain `pip install` outside an environment like this one.

```bash
python3 -m venv ~/extract-text-env
source ~/extract-text-env/bin/activate
pip install "extract-text @ https://github.com/evictionresearch/extract-text/archive/main.zip#subdirectory=python"
```

On Windows, skip the first two lines. The Python that step 1 installs accepts the `pip install` line as it is. On a Mac or Linux, run the `source` line again in every new terminal window, before any `extract-text` command. The install also gives you the `extract-text` command, which steps 5, 6, and 8 use. Check your setup with it.

```bash
extract-text doctor
```

The last line of the checkup should be this one.

```{.output}
Ready: the deterministic engine can run.
```

The checkup lists poppler and tesseract with the folder it found each in. It reports Ollama as missing, and that is fine. Ollama belongs to the experimental AI engine, which these steps do not use.

Then start Python from that same terminal window, with `python`, or point your editor or notebook at `~/extract-text-env`. If this line raises no error, Python has found the engine.

```python
from extract_text import extract, scan
```
::::
:::::

## [3]{.num} Read one example document {#example}

This downloads a made-up summons from the package's test files and reads it.

::::: {.tabs}
:::: {.tab data-tab="r"}
```r
f <- file.path(tempdir(), "synthetic_summons_scanned.pdf")
download.file(paste0("https://raw.githubusercontent.com/evictionresearch/",
                     "extract-text/main/python/tests/fixtures/",
                     "synthetic_summons_scanned.pdf"),
              f, mode = "wb")

# Open the summons, to compare with what the engine reads
browseURL(f)

one <- extract_deterministic(f)

# Expect 1234 EXAMPLE AVE S APT 5, Seattle, WA 98100
one$record$defendant_address

# Problems the engine found; empty means none
one$flags
```
::::

:::: {.tab data-tab="terminal"}
```bash
curl -L -o synthetic_summons_scanned.pdf https://raw.githubusercontent.com/evictionresearch/extract-text/main/python/tests/fixtures/synthetic_summons_scanned.pdf

extract-text extract synthetic_summons_scanned.pdf
```

In PowerShell on Windows, type `curl.exe` in place of `curl`. The first line saves the summons in the folder the terminal is in, where you can open it to compare. The second prints everything the engine read. Look for this part, the defendants' address, and for `"flags": []` near the end, which means the engine found no problem.

```{.output}
    "defendant_address": {
      "raw": "1234 EXAMPLE AVE S APT 5 SEATTLE, WA 98100",
      "street": "1234 EXAMPLE AVE S APT 5",
      "unit": "APT 5",
      "city": "Seattle",
      "state": "WA",
      "zip": "98100"
    },
```
::::

:::: {.tab data-tab="python"}
```python
from urllib.request import urlretrieve
from extract_text import extract

# Saves the summons in the folder Python is running in, where you can open
# it to compare with what the engine reads
f, _ = urlretrieve("https://raw.githubusercontent.com/evictionresearch/"
                   "extract-text/main/python/tests/fixtures/"
                   "synthetic_summons_scanned.pdf",
                   "synthetic_summons_scanned.pdf")

one = extract(f)

# Expect 1234 EXAMPLE AVE S APT 5, Seattle, WA 98100
one.record.defendant_address

# Problems the engine found; empty means none
one.flags
```
::::
:::::

## [4]{.num} Scan a random 50 of your own documents {#sample}

Start with a random sample, not the whole folder. It takes minutes, and you grade every document in it in the next step.

::: {.note}
**Which documents to put in the folder.** The engine reads one document at a time and writes one row for every file, whatever kind of document the file is. Its rules are built for the summons. If your folder holds whole case files (complaints, orders, returns of service), a case gets a row for each of them. When the file names say which documents are summonses, scan those alone, by giving the scan a list of files in place of the folder.

::::: {.tabs}
:::: {.tab data-tab="r"}
```r
summonses <- list.files(docs_dir, pattern = "summons", ignore.case = TRUE,
                        recursive = TRUE, full.names = TRUE)
```

Then give `scan_documents()` the list, `summonses`, in place of `docs_dir`.
::::

:::: {.tab data-tab="terminal"}
```bash
extract-text scan DOCS/*summons* --engine deterministic --sample 50 --seed 1 --out RESULTS/sample
```

On a Mac or Linux, `DOCS/*summons*` names every file in the folder whose name holds "summons". The pattern minds capital letters and does not look in subfolders. PowerShell on Windows does not fill in such a pattern, so there, put the summonses in a folder of their own.
::::

:::: {.tab data-tab="python"}
```python
from pathlib import Path

summonses = sorted(p for p in Path(docs_dir).rglob("*")
                   if p.is_file() and "summons" in p.name.lower())
```

Then give `scan()` the list, `summonses`, in place of `docs_dir`.
::::
:::::
:::

::: {.note}
**If your documents are not from Washington.** The rules that read the city and the state expect "WA" or "Washington" after the city. On a made-up Oregon summons and a made-up Texas one, the engine read the street, the unit, and the ZIP, left the city and state blank, and raised no flag. Every document you grade carries your city and state in the final table, and the others carry the street and ZIP alone. [Documents from another state](https://github.com/evictionresearch/extract-text/blob/main/docs/changing_rules.md#documents-from-another-state){target="_blank" rel="noopener noreferrer"} shows the four-line change that makes the engine read your state.
:::

::: {.note}
**Practice first, on made-up documents.** Steps 4 to 8 run on the package's 15 made-up documents as well as on real ones, so you can learn the grading page before you open a court record. The lines below download the package's code (about 10 MB) into a folder in your home directory. The documents are few and partly repeat one another, so the practice scores mean nothing. Delete the folder when you are done.

::::: {.tabs}
:::: {.tab data-tab="r"}
```r
practice <- path.expand("~/extract_text_practice")
dir.create(practice, showWarnings = FALSE)
download.file(paste0("https://github.com/evictionresearch/extract-text/",
                     "archive/refs/heads/main.zip"),
              file.path(practice, "extract-text.zip"), mode = "wb")
unzip(file.path(practice, "extract-text.zip"), exdir = practice)
docs_dir <- file.path(practice, "extract-text-main", "python", "tests",
                      "fixtures")
results  <- file.path(practice, "results")
```

Run it, skip the `docs_dir` and `results` lines below, and go on from `n_sample`.
::::

:::: {.tab data-tab="terminal"}
```bash
mkdir -p ~/extract_text_practice
cd ~/extract_text_practice
curl -L -o extract-text.zip https://github.com/evictionresearch/extract-text/archive/refs/heads/main.zip
unzip -q extract-text.zip
```

These four lines are for a Mac or Linux. On Windows, open that address in your browser, save the zip in a new folder, and unzip it there. Then, in every line from here on, type `~/extract_text_practice/extract-text-main/python/tests/fixtures` in place of `DOCS` and `~/extract_text_practice/results` in place of `RESULTS`.
::::

:::: {.tab data-tab="python"}
```python
from pathlib import Path
from urllib.request import urlretrieve
from zipfile import ZipFile

practice = Path.home() / "extract_text_practice"
practice.mkdir(exist_ok=True)
urlretrieve("https://github.com/evictionresearch/extract-text/"
            "archive/refs/heads/main.zip",
            practice / "extract-text.zip")
ZipFile(practice / "extract-text.zip").extractall(practice)
docs_dir = practice / "extract-text-main" / "python" / "tests" / "fixtures"
results  = practice / "results"
```

Run it, skip the `docs_dir` and `results` lines below, and go on from `n_sample`.
::::
:::::
:::

You name two folders. The first holds your court documents (PDF or TIFF, subfolders included). If the documents come to you in a Google Drive folder, download the folder to your own computer first (Drive gives a zip; unzip it). The second is a new folder where everything from here on is written. Expect about 5 seconds a document when OCR is needed.

::::: {.tabs}
:::: {.tab data-tab="r"}
`docs_dir` is the documents folder and `results` the results folder. Type each path with forward slashes, on Windows too.

```r
# Mac:     "/Users/yourname/Documents/court_documents"
# Windows: "C:/Users/yourname/Documents/court_documents"
docs_dir <- "path/to/your/documents"
results  <- "path/to/your/results"
n_sample <- 50

sample_dir <- file.path(results, "sample")
all_dir    <- file.path(results, "all")

res <- scan_documents(docs_dir, engine = "deterministic", sample = n_sample,
                      seed = 1, out_dir = sample_dir)
```

When the scan finishes, count what came back.

```r
res %>%
  count(text_source,
        found   = defendant_street != "",
        flagged = flags != "")
```

```{.output}
# A tibble: 3 × 4
  text_source found flagged     n
  <chr>       <lgl> <lgl>   <int>
1 pdf_ocr     FALSE TRUE        1
2 pdf_ocr     TRUE  FALSE       4
3 pdf_ocr     TRUE  TRUE        1
```

This example comes from six made-up documents, so your counts will differ. `found` says whether the engine read a street, and `flagged` says whether it raised a flag. `pdf_ocr` means the pages were scans read by OCR.
::::

:::: {.tab data-tab="terminal"}
In this line and every one after it, type your documents folder in place of `DOCS` and your results folder in place of `RESULTS`. Put quotation marks around a path that has a space in it.

```bash
# Mac:     /Users/yourname/Documents/court_documents
# Windows: C:/Users/yourname/Documents/court_documents
extract-text scan DOCS --engine deterministic --sample 50 --seed 1 --out RESULTS/sample
```

When the scan finishes, it prints the count of what came back.

```{.output}
  scanned 6/6

6 documents scanned, 6 with a defendant street address, 0 flagged for review.
Results in RESULTS/sample/extracted.csv (and extracted.jsonl).
Grade it on the review page with: extract-text review --out RESULTS/sample --serve
```

This example comes from six of the package's made-up practice documents, so your counts will differ. `extracted.csv` is the table, one row per document. Step 5 adds `--random 50` to the line the scan suggests, so that the page shows a random 50.
::::

:::: {.tab data-tab="python"}
`docs_dir` is the documents folder and `results` the results folder. Type each path with forward slashes, on Windows too.

```python
from extract_text import scan

# Mac:     "/Users/yourname/Documents/court_documents"
# Windows: "C:/Users/yourname/Documents/court_documents"
docs_dir = "path/to/your/documents"
results  = "path/to/your/results"
n_sample = 50

sample_dir = f"{results}/sample"
all_dir    = f"{results}/all"

rows = scan(docs_dir, engine="deterministic", sample=n_sample, seed=1,
            out_dir=sample_dir)
```

`rows` is a list with one dictionary per document, and the same table is saved as `extracted.csv` in the sample folder. When the scan finishes, count what came back.

```python
from collections import Counter

Counter((r["text_source"], r["defendant_street"] != "", r["flags"] != "")
        for r in rows)
```

```{.output}
Counter({('image_ocr', True, False): 4, ('pdf_ocr', True, False): 1, ('pdf_text_layer', True, False): 1})
```

This example comes from six of the package's made-up practice documents, so your counts will differ. Each entry gives how the text was read, whether the engine read a street, whether it raised a flag, and how many documents that describes. `image_ocr` and `pdf_ocr` mean the pages were scans read by OCR.
::::
:::::

::: {.note}
**Keep both folders private.** Your documents and every file written from this step on hold tenants' names and addresses. Keep them wherever your organization keeps the court documents themselves, and out of any folder that syncs or is shared (Dropbox, iCloud Drive, OneDrive, or a Google Drive folder that syncs to your computer).
:::

## [5]{.num} Grade the sample, then score the engine {#grade}

Grading is required. Until you grade a sample, you do not know how often the scan is right on your documents.

The line below opens a page in your browser that shows each document beside what the engine read. Check each field against the page, change only what is wrong, and leave a field blank when the document does not have it. Then look at the colored boxes on the page image, which show where the engine read each value. Drag a box that sits over the wrong place to the right one. Where a field has no box, press the field's button under the image and drag across the value. A box you draw is added to the ones already there, and a box in the wrong place is deleted with its cross. Save every document, even when the engine got everything right. The top of the page has the grading rules in brief, and its foot says what to do when you finish. Fifty documents take about an hour.

::::: {.tabs}
:::: {.tab data-tab="r"}
```r
review_documents(res, correct = TRUE, n = n_sample, draw = "random")
```

You can stop at any point by pressing Esc in RStudio, and running the line again picks up where you left off.
::::

:::: {.tab data-tab="terminal"}
```bash
extract-text review --out RESULTS/sample --random 50 --serve
```

The terminal waits while you grade. You can stop at any point by pressing Ctrl-C there, and running the line again picks up where you left off.
::::

:::: {.tab data-tab="python"}
Steps 5, 6, and 8 have no Python function of their own. They use the `extract-text` command, which the install in step 2 put beside the Python package. Run it in a terminal window with the environment from step 2 turned on, and type your results folder in place of `RESULTS`.

```bash
extract-text review --out RESULTS/sample --random 50 --serve
```

The terminal waits while you grade. You can stop at any point by pressing Ctrl-C there, and running the line again picks up where you left off.

```{=html}
<li data-start="3.4">The page is on the left. On the right is what the rules engine read, above a form filled in with its answers.</li>
<li data-start="9.6">The colored boxes show where the engine found each value. Red marks the defendants and blue marks the address.</li>
<li data-start="15.2">Check each field against the page. Here the page prints the city as Sampleton.</li>
<li data-start="19.4">The rules engine misspelled it as Sampieton, so we correct it in the City box of the form.</li>
<li data-start="25.4">The top of the page names the defendants too. We pick Defendants.</li>
<li data-start="29.2">Then we drag a box over those names. Boxes like this teach the engine where the form prints each field.</li>
<li data-start="34.7">Our box is added to the page. The engine's own box, on the line addressed to the defendants, stays where it was.</li>
<li data-start="37.4">A box that sits in the wrong place can be deleted. Point at it and press its cross.</li>
<li data-start="42.3">We press Save. Save every document you check, even when the engine got everything right.</li>
<li data-start="47.6">The page confirms the save and notes that the engine was wrong on the city.</li>
<li data-start="51.3">Your answers stay in a file on your own computer. The full guide is GRADING.md.</li>
</ol>
</details>
</figure>
```

Then score the engine against your answers.

::::: {.tabs}
:::: {.tab data-tab="r"}
```r
score_documents(res)
```

```{.output}
  field      checked right  near blank wrong
1 plaintiff        1     1     0     0     0
2 defendants       1     1     0     0     0
3 street           1     1     0     0     0
4 unit             1     1     0     0     0
5 city             1     0     0     0     1
6 state            1     1     0     0     0
7 zip              1     1     0     0     0
```

This example is the one made-up document graded in the video, where the engine misread the city. It is shortened to the main columns. With 50 graded documents, `checked` reads 50. The score has one row per field and counts how many documents the engine got right, nearly right (the right content written differently, such as Ave for Avenue), left blank, or got wrong. Two more columns, `right_random` and `checked_random`, give the accuracy estimate for the whole folder when you divide the first by the second.
::::

:::: {.tab data-tab="terminal"}
```bash
extract-text score --out RESULTS/sample
```

```{.output}
Corrections in sample: 6 documents reviewed, 0 unreadable, 6 random
Scored against the scan as it is now in that folder.
Graded by yourname (6).

deterministic engine, share of fields right, then right or near (random rows alone in brackets)
  plaintiff        100.0% 100.0% of    6  [100.0% of 6]
  defendants       100.0% 100.0% of    6  [100.0% of 6]
  street            83.3%  83.3% of    6  [83.3% of 6]   wrong: 1 different
  unit              66.7%  66.7% of    6  [66.7% of 6]   wrong: 1 different, 1 blank
  city             100.0% 100.0% of    6  [100.0% of 6]
  state            100.0% 100.0% of    6  [100.0% of 6]
  zip               83.3%  83.3% of    6  [83.3% of 6]   wrong: 1 different
```

This example comes from six of the package's made-up practice documents, two of them graded with a correction. The score has one row per field. The first percentage is the share of graded documents the engine got right. The second adds those it got nearly right (the right content written differently, such as Ave for Avenue), and the number after "of" is how many you checked. The brackets hold the share right among the documents drawn at random, which is the accuracy estimate for the whole folder. The end of a row says how the wrong ones went wrong.
::::

:::: {.tab data-tab="python"}
The score comes from the same command, in the terminal.

```bash
extract-text score --out RESULTS/sample
```

```{.output}
Corrections in sample: 6 documents reviewed, 0 unreadable, 6 random
Scored against the scan as it is now in that folder.
Graded by yourname (6).

deterministic engine, share of fields right, then right or near (random rows alone in brackets)
  plaintiff        100.0% 100.0% of    6  [100.0% of 6]
  defendants       100.0% 100.0% of    6  [100.0% of 6]
  street            83.3%  83.3% of    6  [83.3% of 6]   wrong: 1 different

  city             100.0% 100.0% of    6  [100.0% of 6]
  state            100.0% 100.0% of    6  [100.0% of 6]

```

This example comes from six of the package's made-up practice documents, two of them graded with a correction. The score has one row per field. The first percentage is the share of graded documents the engine got right. The second adds those it got nearly right (the right content written differently, such as Ave for Avenue), and the number after "of" is how many you checked. The brackets hold the share right among the documents drawn at random, which is the accuracy estimate for the whole folder. The end of a row says how the wrong ones went wrong.
::::
:::::

**Reading the score.** Say the street row shows 43 right of 50 checked. The engine read the street right on 86 percent of your sample. Fifty documents is a small sample, so the share for the whole folder is probably between about 76 and 96 percent. Grade 100 or more before you publish counts or send anything to people.

Decide here whether the fields you need are accurate enough to scan everything. No score is right for everyone, so ask what the table is for. A count of filings by ZIP code can live with a street that is wrong one time in seven, and a mailing to tenants cannot. Look only at the fields you will use, and grade those with care, because a field you leave as the engine filled it is counted as right.

When a field you need is weak, there are three things to do.

- **The engine looked in the wrong place.** Its box sat over the wrong part of the page, or the field had no box. Step 6 can fix that for your court's forms, with no code.
- **The box was in the right place and the value was still wrong.** A rule has to change. [Improve it](improve.html) shows how to tell us what goes wrong and how to change a rule on your own copy.
- **Grade more.** Whatever the score, every document you grade is right in the final table. For a small folder, grading all of it is a sound plan.

Your corrections do not change the engine's rules. They tell you which fields to trust, every document you grade carries your answer in the final table, and your boxes teach the engine your court's forms in the next step. [How the rules improve](how-it-works.html#rules) says how the rules themselves get better.

## [6]{.num} Teach the engine your court's forms {#forms}

This step is optional and needs no code. Courts print their own forms, and a form can put the tenant's address where the engine's rules do not look. The boxes you fixed and drew while grading show where your court's forms print each field. From them the package writes a template for each form that has at least five graded documents.

::::: {.tabs}
:::: {.tab data-tab="r"}
```r
learn_templates(res)

# Opens a page showing each template over a page it was learned from
review_templates(res)

# Approve each template whose regions sit where the form prints that field
approve_template("form-1", res)
```
::::

:::: {.tab data-tab="terminal"}
```bash
extract-text templates learn --out RESULTS/sample

# Writes a page showing each template over a page it was learned from, and
# prints where the page is. Open that file in your browser.
extract-text templates review --templates RESULTS/sample/templates --out RESULTS/sample

# Approve each template whose regions sit where the form prints that field
extract-text templates approve form-1 --templates RESULTS/sample/templates
```
::::

:::: {.tab data-tab="python"}
These are terminal commands too.

```bash
extract-text templates learn --out RESULTS/sample

# Writes a page showing each template over a page it was learned from, and
# prints where the page is. Open that file in your browser.
extract-text templates review --templates RESULTS/sample/templates --out RESULTS/sample

# Approve each template whose regions sit where the form prints that field
extract-text templates approve form-1 --templates RESULTS/sample/templates
```
::::
:::::

Nothing learned is used until you approve it. A template holds the form's printed words and a region of the page for each field. It holds no names or addresses.

Expect templates only for the forms your court uses most. A random 50 rarely holds five documents of a rare form, and the engine reads those with its rules alone. A template changes where the engine looks, not how it reads. [Form templates](how-it-works.html#templates) says more.

## [7]{.num} Scan the whole folder and grade a second 50 {#full}

The full run goes to its own folder, so the sample and its corrections stay as they are. It uses the templates you approved in step 6, and the rules alone if you approved none. It needs no attention while it runs. At about 5 seconds a document, 4,000 documents take five or six hours.

::::: {.tabs}
:::: {.tab data-tab="r"}
```r
templates_dir <- file.path(sample_dir, "templates")
use_templates <- dir.exists(templates_dir) &&
  any(list_templates(templates_dir)$approved)

res_all <- scan_documents(docs_dir, engine = "deterministic", out_dir = all_dir,
                          templates = if (use_templates) templates_dir)
```
::::

:::: {.tab data-tab="terminal"}
```bash
# Leave off --templates and what follows it if you approved none in step 6
extract-text scan DOCS --engine deterministic --out RESULTS/all --templates RESULTS/sample/templates
```
::::

:::: {.tab data-tab="python"}
```python
# If you approved a template in step 6
rows_all = scan(docs_dir, engine="deterministic", out_dir=all_dir,
                templates=f"{sample_dir}/templates")

# If you approved none
rows_all = scan(docs_dir, engine="deterministic", out_dir=all_dir)
```

Run one of the two. The first stops with an error when the folder holds no approved template, so that a run without templates is never mistaken for one with them.
::::
:::::

The first sample told you whether to run everything. A second sample measures the run that becomes your table, templates included. A document you already graded may come up again; grade it again, and the later answer is the one kept.

::::: {.tabs}
:::: {.tab data-tab="r"}
```r
review_documents(res_all, correct = TRUE, n = n_sample, draw = "random", seed = 1)

score_documents(res_all)
```
::::

:::: {.tab data-tab="terminal"}
```bash
extract-text review --out RESULTS/all --random 50 --serve

extract-text score --out RESULTS/all
```
::::

:::: {.tab data-tab="python"}
Grade and score in the terminal, as in step 5.

```bash
extract-text review --out RESULTS/all --random 50 --serve

extract-text score --out RESULTS/all
```
::::
:::::

The share right in this score is the accuracy of the full run. Report it with the table.

You can also fix every document the engine flagged, so the table carries a person's answer wherever the engine was unsure.

::::: {.tabs}
:::: {.tab data-tab="r"}
```r
review_documents(res_all, correct = TRUE, n = sum(res_all$flags != ""),
                 draw = "flagged")
```
::::

:::: {.tab data-tab="terminal"}
```bash
extract-text review --out RESULTS/all --n 200 --serve
```

Without `--random`, the page shows flagged documents first. `--n` is how many documents it shows, 30 if you leave it off, so give it a number at least as large as the count of flagged documents the scan printed.
::::

:::: {.tab data-tab="python"}
```bash
extract-text review --out RESULTS/all --n 200 --serve
```

Without `--random`, the page shows flagged documents first. `--n` is how many documents it shows, 30 if you leave it off, so give it a number at least as large as the count of flagged documents the scan printed.
::::
:::::

## [8]{.num} Build the final table {#table}

::::: {.tabs}
:::: {.tab data-tab="r"}
```r
cases <- case_table(res_all, graded = sample_dir,
                    save = file.path(results, "case_table.csv"))

# How many rows carry a graded answer, and how many the engine's reading
count(cases, source)
```

```{.output}
# A tibble: 2 × 2
  source     n
  <chr>  <int>
1 engine     5
2 graded     1
```

In this example, from six made-up documents, one row carries a graded answer and five carry the engine's reading.
::::

:::: {.tab data-tab="terminal"}
```bash
extract-text case-table --out RESULTS/all --graded RESULTS/sample --save RESULTS/case_table.csv
```

```{.output}
Table saved to RESULTS/case_table.csv
Documents in the table: 15 (9 engine, 6 graded)
```

In this example, from the package's 15 made-up practice documents, six rows carry a graded answer and nine carry the engine's reading.
::::

:::: {.tab data-tab="python"}
The table is built by a terminal command.

```bash
extract-text case-table --out RESULTS/all --graded RESULTS/sample --save RESULTS/case_table.csv
```

```{.output}
Table saved to RESULTS/case_table.csv
Documents in the table: 15 (9 engine, 6 graded)
```

In this example, from the package's 15 made-up practice documents, six rows carry a graded answer and nine carry the engine's reading.

To go on working with the table in Python, read the file.

```python
import csv

with open(f"{results}/case_table.csv", newline="", encoding="utf-8") as f:
    cases = list(csv.DictReader(f))
```
::::
:::::

The table has one row per document, with the case number, the plaintiff, the defendants, and the defendants' address. Your graded answers from both samples replace the engine's wherever you gave one, and the `source` column says which each row carries. The table is saved as `case_table.csv` in your results folder.

## If something goes wrong {#help}

**Run the checkup first.** `extracttext_doctor()` in R, or `extract-text doctor` at a terminal, looks at your computer and prints the command for anything missing.

**In R, the checkup says "The Python engine is not installed yet."** Restart R and run it again. If the message stays, the install in step 2 stopped early, most often because Python was missing or older than 3.10. Run the Python check in step 2 and fix what it shows. Then remove the half-built environment with `reticulate::virtualenv_remove("r-extracttext")` and run `extracttext_install()` again.

If the install finished and the message still stays, something has told R to use another Python. In a fresh R session, point R at the engine's own environment before anything else, then run the checkup.

```r
library(extracttext)
reticulate::use_virtualenv("r-extracttext", required = TRUE)
extracttext_doctor()
```

**At a terminal, `extract-text` gives "command not found".** The environment from step 2 is not turned on in this window. On a Mac or Linux, run `source ~/extract-text-env/bin/activate` and try again.

**Something else.** Open an issue at [github.com/evictionresearch/extract-text/issues](https://github.com/evictionresearch/extract-text/issues){target="_blank" rel="noopener noreferrer"}, or write to [evictions@berkeley.edu](mailto:evictions@berkeley.edu).

::: {.note}
**Never paste a real document, name, address, or case number into an issue or an email.** Describe the problem, or reproduce it with the made-up example document from step 3.
:::
